---
title: "`cd` — synthetic control under a known spillover structure"
subtitle: "Cao & Dowd (v3): all-unit synthetic controls, an exposure matrix, and end-of-sample inference"
---

`cd` implements Jianfei Cao and Connor Dowd's *Estimation and Inference for
Synthetic Control Methods with Spillover Effects*
([arXiv:1902.07343v3](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.07343v3)). The
[model catalogue](index.qmd) compares it with the default
[`sar` model](sar.qmd). This page states the model, the estimator, the
inference, and the tools for checking the assumed structure. It also
documents where scspill's defaults differ from the authors' application
code. The implementation was contributed by Hayato Tagawa.

Select it with `method="cd"` in `SCSPILLConfig`. Every field that only `cd`
reads is marked `(method='cd')` in the
[API reference](../reference/SCSPILLConfig.qmd).

## Setup

Units $i = 1, \dots, N$ are observed over periods $t = 1, \dots, T$; unit $1$
is treated from period $T_0 + 1$ onward. SUTVA is not assumed: the treatment
may change the outcomes of other units too. Collect the effects of period $t$
in one vector,
$$
\alpha_t = Y_t - Y_t(\mathbf 0) \in \mathbb R^N ,
$$
whose first entry is the **treatment effect** on unit $1$ and whose other
entries are the **spillover effects** on the controls. Classical synthetic
control estimates only the first entry, and it does so assuming every other
entry is zero.

## The spillover model

Cao and Dowd take the structure of the spillovers as known up to a few
parameters (v3 Section 2.2):
$$
\alpha_t = A\,\gamma_t , \qquad A \in \mathbb R^{N \times k},\ k < N .
$$
The exposure matrix $A$ states who can be affected and how; $\gamma_t$ holds
the magnitudes, free in every period. scspill builds $A$ from
`spillover_structure`:

| `spillover_structure` | Paper | $A$ | Parameters $\gamma_t$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"per_unit"` (default) | Example 1 (Section 2.2): limited range | one indicator column per treated unit and per unit in `affected_units` | the direct effect, then one spillover per exposed control |
| `"homogeneous"` | Example 2 (Section 3.4) | one indicator column per treated unit, then one column of ones on `affected_units` | the direct effect and one spillover shared by the exposed controls |
| `"distance_decay"` | Example 3 (Section 7.1) | one indicator column per treated unit, then $e^{-d_i}$ for each control in `unit_distances` | the direct effect and $b$, the spillover at distance zero |
| `"custom"` | any $A$ | the labeled `effect_matrix` | one per column |

Controls with a zero row of $A$ are the *pure donors*: they are assumed
unexposed. A custom `effect_matrix` must give each treated unit its own
direct-effect column: a single 1 in that unit's row, and zeros in every other
row. scspill rejects anything else, because a spillover column that also
loads on the treated unit would leak into its effect.

**Several treated units.** Units that switch on in the same period are all
treated (v3 Section S.1.2). Each gets its own direct-effect column, and
`att_by_unit` reports every one. The headline surface (`att`,
`counterfactual`, the plots) follows the first treated unit in label order.
Staggered adoption is rejected.

## Estimation

**All-unit synthetic controls.** Every unit $i$, treated or not, gets an
intercept and simplex weights on all the other units, fitted on the
pre-treatment periods:
$$
(\hat a_i, \hat b_i) = \arg\min_{a,\ b \in \Delta_{-i}}
  \sum_{t \le T_0} \bigl(y_{it} - a - Y_t' b\bigr)^2 ,
$$
where $\Delta_{-i}$ is the unit simplex with $b_i = 0$ (Section 3). Stack them
into $\hat a$ and $\hat B$, and write $R = I - \hat B$. Before treatment the
residuals $\hat u_t = R Y_t - \hat a$ are pure noise. After treatment, the
effects enter through $R$:
$$
R Y_t - \hat a = R A \gamma_t + u_t .
$$

**The estimator.** Least squares in that equation (Section 3.2) gives
$$
\hat\gamma_t = (A' R' R A)^{-1} A' R' (R Y_t - \hat a),
\qquad
\hat\alpha_t = A \hat\gamma_t .
$$
It is identified when $RA$ has full column rank, so $A'MA$ with $M = R'R$ is
invertible (Section 3.4). One case always fails: every row of $\hat B$ sums
to one, so $R\mathbf 1 = 0$, and a structure that gives *every* control the
same spillover is unidentified. scspill checks the rank and names the
failure.

**The efficient estimator.** Weighting the residual equations by a matrix
$W$ gives
$\hat\gamma_W = (A' R' W R A)^{-1} A' R' W (R Y_t - \hat a)$. With $W$ a
consistent estimate of $\Omega^{-1}$, where $\Omega$ is the covariance of
$u_t$, its asymptotic variance is never larger (Section S.1.1, Proposition
S.1). `weighting="efficient"` adds it to the fit as `result.cd.efficient`,
alongside the headline estimator. It uses
$\hat\Omega = T_0^{-1}\sum_t \hat u_t \hat u_t' + 10^{-6} I$, and it warns
when $T_0$ does not exceed the number of units: $\hat\Omega$ is then singular
without that ridge.

## Inference

**The P test.** Andrews' (2003) end-of-sample instability test, generalized
to $H_0: C\alpha_t = d$ (Section 4.2). The statistic is
$$
P = (C\hat\alpha_t - d)'\, W\, (C\hat\alpha_t - d),
$$
and its null distribution is approximated by the same quadratic form on the
pre-treatment placebo effects, $\hat P_s = \hat u_s' \hat G' C' W C \hat G
\hat u_s$, $s = 1, \dots, T_0$, with $\hat G = A(A'MA)^{-1}A'R'$. The test
rejects when $P$ exceeds the $(1-\tau)$-quantile of the references, defined
as the left inverse of their empirical CDF,
$\inf\{x : \hat F(x) \ge 1-\tau\}$. The P value is the share of references at
least as large as $P$. `result.test_hypothesis(C, d=..., period=...)` runs
any such test, with $W$ the identity, a matrix you pass, or
`weight="inverse_covariance"`.

**Pointwise results.** For every unit and post-treatment period,
`pointwise_p_values` tests $\alpha_{it} = 0$, and `effect_ci` holds the
interval obtained by inverting that test: $\hat\alpha_{it} \pm
\sqrt{q_{1-\tau}}$, with $q_{1-\tau}$ the critical value of the squared
placebo effects. The interval is symmetric, and with several post periods
each one is treated as the year right after the intervention (Section
S.1.3). There is no interval for the average effect, so `att_ci` is `None`.

**Reference statistics.** By default the references come from the
full-sample fit, as Section 4 defines them. `reference_mode=
"leave_one_period_out"` refits every SCM equation without each pre-treatment
period and evaluates the refit on the period left out, a construction the
paper points to in Andrews (2003) and Andrews and Kim (2006). In the
Proposition 99 application it widens the intervals considerably.

## Checking the structure

**The $\kappa_A$ test** (Section 5.1.2). If $A$ is right, the part of the
post-treatment residual that $RA$ cannot explain is noise like the
pre-treatment residuals:
$$
\kappa_A = \lVert (I - \hat\Gamma_A)(R Y_t - \hat a) \rVert ,
\qquad
\hat\Gamma_A = RA(A'R'RA)^{-1}A'R' .
$$
Its references are $\lVert (I - \hat\Gamma_A)\hat u_s \rVert$, and
`result.kappa_test[period]` reports the test in every post period.

**Choosing a structure** (Sections 5.1.2 and S.1.3).
`result.select_structure_by_kappa(candidates)` compares candidate structures
on the same SCM fit and picks the smallest statistic. The default statistic
is the paper's multi-period one,
$\lVert \sum_s (I - \hat\Gamma_A)(R Y_{T_0+s} - \hat a) \rVert / \sqrt{T_1}$,
under which selection is consistent as the post period grows.
`statistic="mean_norm"` averages the per-period norms instead, as mlsynth
does. A structure that nests another always fits at least as well, so
compare candidates of similar size.

**Sensitivity to missed spillovers** (Section 5.2.2). Suppose $p$ of the
controls assumed clean in fact receive spillovers no larger than
$\bar\alpha$. The asymptotic bias of the direct effect is then at most
$c_p\,\bar\alpha$. Here $c_p$ is the sum of the $p$ largest absolute weights
in one of two sets:

- for the spillover-aware estimator, the treated unit's row of
  $\hat G R - I$ over the clean controls (Section 5.1.1);
- for the *pure-donor* synthetic control, which drops every exposed unit from
  the donor pool, its donor weights.

`result.cd.sensitivity` holds both weight vectors, and `plot(kind=
"sensitivity")` draws the bounds, the paper's Figure 3.

## Fit

```python
from scspill import SCSPILL
from scspill.data import load_california_cd

panel = load_california_cd(51)        # 50 states + DC, 1970–2000, treated from 1989
result = SCSPILL({**panel.config_kwargs(), "display_graphs": False}).fit()
```

| Accessor | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `result.att`, `result.counterfactual`, `result.gap` | the headline treated unit, from the shared effect surface |
| `result.effects_panel` | every unit's effect by post period: treated columns direct, control columns spillovers |
| `result.effect_ci[unit]`, `result.pointwise_p_values` | pointwise intervals and P values |
| `result.test_hypothesis(C, d=0, period=1990)` | any linear hypothesis $C\alpha_t = d$ |
| `result.kappa_test`, `result.select_structure_by_kappa(...)` | the structure test, and choosing among structures |
| `result.cd.sensitivity`, `result.cd.efficient` | the sensitivity weights; the efficient estimator |
| `result.scm_matrix`, `result.intercepts`, `result.effect_matrix` | $\hat B$, $\hat a$, $A$ |
| `result.plot(kind=...)` | `panel`, `full`, `effect`, `spill_top`, `weights`, `spillover`, `kappa`, `sensitivity` |

The [Proposition 99 case study](../prop99-spillovers.qmd) walks through all
of it and sets `cd` beside `sar`. [The `cd` model in practice](../articles/cd-results.qmd)
goes further: it separates model from sample in the `cd`/`sar` comparison,
and it diagnoses why the structure test rejects.

## Where scspill departs from the authors' code {#departures}

`cd` defaults to the paper's definitions. The authors' Proposition 99
application code ([jcao0/synthetic-control-spillover](https://github.com/jcao0/synthetic-control-spillover)
at commit `86004020`) differs in two places. Each has a switch, so its
published numbers can be reproduced:

| # | Authors' application code | scspill default (v3 Section 4) | Switch |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | critical value: NumPy's linearly interpolated quantile of the references | the left inverse of their empirical CDF | `quantile_method="linear"` |
| 2 | interval: the estimate plus the signed placebo quantiles, $\hat\alpha + [q_{\tau/2}, q_{1-\tau/2}]$ | inversion of the squared P test, symmetric about $\hat\alpha$ | `ci_method="published"` |

What each changes in practice:

1. **Critical values.** With 19 pre-treatment years, the left inverse is the
   19th order statistic, the largest reference. The interpolated quantile
   sits at position 18.1, just above the second largest. For the joint test
   of "no spillover anywhere" in the 51-unit application, that decides 1994
   and 1995: their statistics fall between the two cut-offs. The authors'
   simulation code uses the left inverse, as the paper does.
2. **Intervals.** Since $\hat\alpha - \alpha \approx G u$, a percentile
   interval would *subtract* the placebo quantiles. Adding them agrees with
   that only when the placebo distribution is symmetric. The paper's own
   Figure 2 uses intervals built by inverting the test (Section 6.2), the
   scspill default.

`published_ci` and `pointwise_ci` are both always stored; `effect_ci` returns
the one `ci_method` selects. The [replication article](../articles/cd-replication.qmd)
shows each setting reproducing its source.

**Compared with mlsynth.** mlsynth's `SPILLSYNTH(method="cd")` implements the
same estimator. scspill matches it to solver tolerance, with identical P
values, using mlsynth's inference settings (those of the application code).
Two differences remain:

- scspill defaults to the paper's inference rather than the application
  code's;
- structure selection uses the paper's multi-period $\kappa_A$ by default,
  where mlsynth averages the per-period norms (`statistic="mean_norm"`).

Covariates, time-varying structures and staggered adoption are outside this
implementation.

## References

The `cd` model implements the method developed by Jianfei Cao and Connor Dowd
in the first reference below.

- Cao, J., & Dowd, C. *Estimation and Inference for Synthetic Control
  Methods with Spillover Effects.* arXiv:1902.07343v3.
  <https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.07343v3>
- Andrews, D. W. K. (2003). End-of-sample instability tests.
  *Econometrica* 71:1661–1694.
- Andrews, D. W. K., & Kim, J. (2006). Tests for cointegration breakdown over
  a short time period. *Journal of Business & Economic Statistics*
  24:379–394.
- Abadie, A., Diamond, A., & Hainmueller, J. (2010). Synthetic control
  methods for comparative case studies. *JASA* 105(490).
- Ferman, B., & Pinto, C. (2019). Inference in differences-in-differences
  with few treated groups and heteroskedasticity. *The Review of Economics
  and Statistics* 101:452–467.
